en: The *Nyāyapraveśaka-sūtra* [states]:
"Proof and refutation, along with their fallacies, are for the sake of informing others;
perception and inference, along with their fallacies, are for the sake of one's own knowledge."
—Thus is the summary of the meaning of the treatise.
In that context, the statements of the thesis and so forth constitute the proof (*sādhana*).
For it is by means of the statements of the thesis, the reason, and the example that a matter not yet understood by the judges (*prāśnika*) is established.

In this context, the "subject" (*pakṣa*) is a locus (*dharmin*) that is well-known, which is intended by the proponent himself as something to be proven (*sādhya*) as qualified by a well-known attribute (*prasiddhaviśeṣa*).
The phrase "not contradicted by perception and so forth" is the ellipsis to be supplied.
For example:
Is sound eternal or non-eternal?
The reason has three characteristics. What, then, are these three characteristics?
They are: presence in the subject (pakṣadharmatva), presence in the similar instances (sapakṣe sattva), and absence in the dissimilar instances (vipakṣe 'sattva).
What, then, is the similar class (sapakṣa),
and what is the dissimilar class (vipakṣa)?
The similar instance (sapakṣa) is an object that possesses the general property of the probandum (sādhyadharma). For example,
when sound is to be proven impermanent, an impermanent object such as a jar is the similar instance.
The counter-example (*vipakṣa*) is that wherein the property to be proven (*sādhya*) is absent.
For instance, "whatever is eternal is seen to be unproduced, as is the case with space.

In this context, the property of being produced (*kṛtakatva*) or the property of following immediately after effort (*prayatnānantarīyakatva*) exists only in the similar example (*sapakṣa*) and is entirely absent from the counter-example.
Thus, this is the reason regarding impermanence and so forth.
The example is of two kinds:
by similarity and by dissimilarity.
In that regard, first by way of similarity (*sādharmya*): where the existence of the reason (*hetu*) only in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) is demonstrated. For example:
Whatever is produced is seen to be impermanent, such as a jar and so forth.
Also by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*):
where the non-existence of the reason is stated precisely when there is the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*). For example:
That which is eternal is seen to be uncreated, just like space.
Here, by the word "eternal" (nitya), the absence of non-eternality is expressed;
and by the word "uncreated" (akṛtaka), the absence of createdness is expressed.
Just as the non-existence of existence is itself non-existence.
The sides and so forth have been explained.
The statements of these [components] constitute the proof at the time of communicating to another.
For example: "Sound is impermanent" is the statement of the thesis (*pakṣavacana*).
"Because it is produced" is the statement of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*).

"Whatever is produced is seen to be impermanent, such as a jar and so forth" is the statement of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) with the similar instances (*sapakṣa*). "Whatever is permanent is seen to be unproduced, such as space" is the statement of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).
These alone are called the three members [of a syllogism].
Furthermore, even that which is intended to be proven is a fallacious thesis (*pakṣābhāsa*) if it contradicts perception and other means of valid cognition.
For example:
1. Contradicted by direct perception, 2. contradicted by inference, 3. contradicted by scripture.
4. Contradictory to the world, 5. Contradictory to one's own words, 6. Having an unestablished qualification.
7. One where the subject is unestablished (aprasiddhaviśeṣya), 8. one where both are unestablished (aprasiddhobhaya), and 9. one where the relation is unestablished (prasiddhasambandha).
Among these, an example of that which contradicts direct perception is:
"Sound is inaudible."
An example of that which is contradicted by inference (*anumānaviruddha*) is:
"A jar is eternal."
An example of that which contradicts scripture is as follows:
for a Vaiśeṣika who seeks to prove that sound is eternal.
An example of what is contrary to worldly consensus (*lokaviruddha*) is as follows:
"A human skull is pure because it is a part of a living being, like a conch shell or a mother-of-pearl."
An example of a [proposition] contradicted by one's own words is:
"My mother is barren.
An example of one whose qualifier is unestablished is a Buddhist stating to a Sāṃkhya: "Sound is perishable."
An example of one whose subject is not established [for the opponent] is:
"The self is conscious," addressed by a Sāṃkhya to a Buddhist.
An example where both [the proponent and the opponent] lack established knowledge is as follows:
for a Vaiśeṣika, against a Buddhist, [arguing] that "the self is the inherent cause of pleasure and so forth."
An example of a well-known relationship is:
"Sound is audible."

The defects of their propositions (*pratijñādoṣa*) are as follows: because it is impossible to establish [their position] by means of refuting the very nature of phenomena (*dharmasvarūpa*), and because their proof (*sādhana*) is futile.
The fallacies of proof have been explained.
The fallacious reasons (hetvābhāsa) are the unestablished (asiddha), the inconclusive (anaikāntika), and the contradictory (viruddha).
Among those, the unestablished (asiddha) is of four types, namely: unestablished for both (ubhayāsiddha), 1;
The unestablished [reason] is of four kinds: (1) unestablished for one of the two parties, (2) doubtful-unestablished, (3) unestablished in its own nature, and (4) unestablished in its locus.
In that case, when the impermanence of sound is to be proven, the reason "because it is visible" is unestablished for both [the proponent and the opponent].

The reason "because of being produced" (kṛtakatvāt) is unestablished for one of the two parties (anyatarāsiddha) when directed against the proponent of the theory that sound is manifested (śabdābhivyaktivādin).
A collection of elements that is being doubted—due to its appearance as vapor and so forth—when adduced for the purpose of proving fire, is "unestablished due to doubt" (saṃdigdhāsiddha).
The argument "space is liquid because it is a substratum of qualities" is "unestablished in its locus" (āśrayāsiddha) against one who denies the existence of space.
The inconclusive [reason] is of six kinds:
the common (sādhāraṇa) and the uncommon (asādhāraṇa).

3. That which exists in one part of the similar instances (sapakṣa) and pervades all dissimilar instances (vipakṣa); 4. That which exists in one part of the dissimilar instances and pervades all similar instances;
5. That which exists in one part of both [similar and dissimilar] instances.
And the contradictory non-erroneous [reason] (viruddhāvyabhicārī) is the sixth.
In that regard, a common [inconclusive] reason is: "Sound is eternal because it is knowable.
For this is inconclusive (anaikāntika) because it is common to both the eternal and non-eternal positions.
Is sound non-eternal because it is knowable like a jar, or is it eternal because it is knowable like space?
"Because it is not common [to both], it is eternal"—

this is a cause for doubt. For that [property of audibility] is excluded from both the categories of the eternal and the non-eternal, and since nothing else exists that is free from being either eternal or non-eternal,
it is a cause for uncertainty as to what kind of thing this audibility belongs to.
An example of that which exists in one part of the similar class (sapakṣa) and pervades the dissimilar class (vipakṣa) is as follows:
"Sound is not produced by an effort [other than its own cause], because it is impermanent.
Here, "not produced by an effort" is the subject (pakṣa).
For this [reason], lightning, space, and so forth constitute the similar instances (*sapakṣa*).
Among these, impermanence exists in some parts, such as lightning, but not in others, such as space.
That which does not follow immediately after an effort is the subject (*pakṣa*).
The counter-example (*vipakṣa*) for this is the jar and so forth.
Impermanence exists in all such cases, including jars and the like.
Therefore, this [reason] is also inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to its commonality with both lightning and the jar.
Is sound produced immediately after effort because it is non-eternal like a jar, or is it produced immediately after effort because it is non-eternal like lightning and so forth?
An example of a reason that occurs in one part of the dissimilar instances (vipakṣa) while pervading all similar instances (sapakṣa) is as follows:
"Sound is produced immediately after effort, because it is impermanent.
Here, "produced immediately after effort" is the subject (pakṣa).
A pot and the like are the similar instances (sapakṣa) for this [reason].
Impermanence exists in all such things as pots.
That which arises immediately after effort is the subject (pakṣa).
For this [reasoning], the counter-examples (*vipakṣa*) are lightning, space, and so forth.
Among these, impermanence exists in one part—namely, in lightning and the like—but not in space and the like.
Therefore, this too is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), just as before, due to the commonality between lightning and a pot.
An example of that which subsists in only one part of both sides is:
"Sound is eternal because it is incorporeal.
Here, "eternal" is the subject (pakṣa).
Space, atoms, and so forth are its similar instances (*sapakṣa*).
Among these, incorporeality exists in some parts, such as space and the like, but not in the atom.
The subject (*pakṣa*) is eternal.
The counter-example (vipakṣa) for this is the jar, pleasure, and so forth.
Here, incorporeality exists in one part [of the subject], namely in pleasure and the like, but not in the jar and so forth.
Therefore, this too is inconclusive (anaikāntika) due to its commonality with both pleasure and space.
An example of the contradictory non-erroneous (*viruddhāvyabhicārī*) [reason] is as follows:
"Sound is impermanent because it is produced, like a pot";
and "Sound is permanent because it is audible, like the nature of sound (*śabdatva*)."
Because both serve as causes for doubt, these two together constitute a single inconclusive reason (*anaikāntika*).
The contradictory [reason] is of four kinds, namely: 1.
that which establishes the opposite of the nature of the property (dharma).

2. Proving the opposite of a specific property of the subject (dharmaviśeṣaviparītasādhana); 3. Proving the opposite of the essential nature of the subject (dharmisvarūpaviparītasādhana); and 4. Proving the opposite of a specific property of the subject (dharmiviśeṣaviparītasādhana).
Among these, an example of a reason that proves the opposite of the nature of the property (*dharmasvarūpaviparītasādhana*) is as follows:
"Sound is eternal, because it is produced, and because it follows immediately after effort.
This reason is contradictory (*viruddha*) because it exists only in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*).
An example of a reason that proves the opposite of a specific property (*dharmaviśeṣaviparītasādhana*) is as follows:
"The eyes and other [senses] exist for the sake of another, because they are composite, like the parts of a bed, a seat, and so forth.
This reason, while proving that the eyes and others exist for the sake of another, likewise proves the compositeness of that other, namely the Self (*ātman*).
Because there is no deviation in either case.
An example of a reason that proves the opposite of the subject's own nature (*dharmisvarūpaviparītasādhana*) is as follows:

"Existence (*bhāva*) is not a substance, nor an action, nor a quality, because it resides in a single substance and because it exists in qualities and actions, like a particular universal (*sāmānyaviśeṣa*).
For this reason, just as it establishes the negation of [being] a substance and so forth for existence, it likewise establishes the non-existence (*abhāvatva*) of existence itself.
Because there is no deviation in either case.
An example of a reason that proves the opposite of a specific property of the subject (*dharmiviśeṣaviparītasādhana*) is as follows:
this very same reason, in this very same prima facie argument, proves the opposite of that specific property of this very same subject— which is called "being the cause of true cognition"— namely,
"being the cause of false cognition," because it does not deviate from either [of these two properties].
The fallacious example is of two kinds:
by way of similarity and by way of dissimilarity.
In that regard, first, there are five types of fallacious examples by way of similarity (*sādharmya*).
They are as follows: (1) that in which the property of the probans (*sādhana-dharma*) is unestablished;...
2. The unestablished property of the probandum (sādhyadharmāsiddha); 3. The unestablished property of both (ubhayadharmāsiddha); 4. The lack of positive concomitance (ananvaya).
And [the fallacy of] inverted positive concomitance (viparītānvaya). 5.
Among these, the unestablished reason (*sādhanadharmāsiddha*) is as follows:
"Sound is eternal because it is incorporeal, like an atom;
for whatever is incorporeal is seen to be eternal, as in the case of an atom."
For in the case of an atom, while the property to be proven—eternality—is present, the probans-property—incorporeality—is absent, because atoms possess corporeality.
An example of one where the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is unestablished is as follows:
"Sound is eternal because it is incorporeal, like cognition;
for whatever is incorporeal is seen to be eternal, as is the case with cognition."

For in the case of the intellect (*buddhi*), the property of the means (*sādhana-dharma*)—immateriality (*amūrtatva*)—is present, but the property of the probandum (*sādhya-dharma*)—eternality (*nityatva*)—is absent;
this is because the intellect is non-eternal.
The unestablished for both [the proponent and the opponent] is of two kinds: existent and non-existent. Among these, "like a jar" is an example of the existent unestablished for both.
Because of its impermanence and its corporeality, the pot [is not eternal];
"like space"— this [example] is unestablished in both respects for one who maintains that [space] does not exist.
Non-concomitance (*ananvaya*) occurs where the coexistence of the probandum and the probans is demonstrated without positive concomitance (*anvaya*).
For example: "In a jar, both being produced and impermanence are observed."
An inverted positive concomitance (*viparītānvaya*) is as follows:
when one ought to say, "Whatever is produced is seen to be impermanent," one instead says, "Whatever is impermanent is seen to be produced."
There are also five types of fallacious examples by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*). They are as follows:
(1) that from which the property to be proven (*sādhya*) is not excluded; 1.
2. Not excluded from the locus of the probandum;
3. not excluded from both;
4. lack of negative concomitance (avyatireka).
And the reversed negative concomitance (viparītavyatireka). 5.
Among these, an example of that which does not exclude the probandum (*sādhyāvyāvṛtta*) is as follows:
"Sound is eternal because it is incorporeal, like an atom. [The opponent argues:
"Whatever is non-eternal is seen to be corporeal, as is the case with an atom."
For, in the case of the atom, the property of the probans—immateriality—is excluded from the atoms because they possess materiality;
however, the property of the probandum—eternality—is not excluded from the atoms because they possess eternality.
An example of that which is excluded from the non-probandum is as follows:
"like an action" (*karmavat*).
In this case, the property of permanence, which is to be proved (*sādhya*) for an action, is excluded [from actions].
Because action is impermanent,
the property of being a means to proof— namely, incorporeality— is not excluded;
for action is incorporeal.
"Not excluded from either" [is the reason],
"like space," [stated] with respect to one who asserts its existence.
Consequently, eternality and incorporeality are not excluded [from the subject],
because space possesses both eternality and incorporeality.
Non-separation (*avyatireka*) occurs where the absence of the subject of the thesis (*sādhya*) and the means of proof (*sādhana*) is demonstrated without [the absence of] their opposites;
for example, "in a jar, both corporeality and impermanence are observed."
An inverted negative concomitance (*viparītavyatireka*) is as follows:
when one ought to say, "Whatever is impermanent is seen to be corporeal," one instead says, "Whatever is corporeal is seen to be impermanent."
The statements of these fallacious propositions, reasons, and examples constitute a fallacious proof.
However, for the purpose of one's own realization, there are only two means of valid cognition: perception and inference.

Among these, perception (*pratyakṣa*) is that cognition which is free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*), being devoid of conceptualizations such as name, genus, and so forth, with respect to an object such as form.
It is called "perception" because it occurs in relation to each sense faculty (*akṣa*).
Inference is the perception of an object through a mark (liṅga).
The mark, moreover, has been described as possessing three characteristics.
Therefore, that cognition which arises regarding the object to be inferred—such as "there is fire here" or "sound is impermanent"—is inference.
In both cases, that very cognition is the result, because it consists in the apprehension [of the object];
its status as a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is due to its appearing as if endowed with an operation.
Conceptual cognition (*kalpanājñāna*) is a semblance of perception (*pratyakṣābhāsa*).

That cognition which arises for one who conceptualizes "this is a jar" or "this is a cloth" is a semblance of perception because it does not have the specific individuality (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the object as its domain.
Knowledge preceded by a fallacious reason (hetvābhāsa) is fallacious inference (anumānābhāsa).
For it has been stated that fallacious reasons are of many kinds;
therefore, whatever knowledge regarding the object to be inferred arises for one who lacks proficiency [in logic], that is fallacious inference.
Refutations are the pointing out of faults in a proof.
A defect of the proof (*sādhana*) is deficiency (*nyūnatva*). A defect of the thesis (*pakṣa*) is contradiction with perception and other means of valid cognition (*pratyakṣādiviruddhatva*).
A defect of the reason (*hetu*) is being unestablished (*asiddha*), inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), or contradictory (*viruddha*).

A defect of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadoṣa*) consists in the non-establishment of the property of the probans (*sādhanadharma*) and so forth. The pointing out of such a defect is a refutation (*dūṣaṇa*), which serves to inform the opponent.
The pointing out of defects in a proof that is not real constitutes fallacious refutations (dūṣaṇābhāsa).
Stating a deficiency when the proof is complete; stating a fault in the thesis when the thesis is not defective; and stating that the reason is unestablished when the reason is established.
A statement based on an inconclusive reason when the reason is actually conclusive;
a statement based on a contradictory reason when the reason is actually non-contradictory;
and a statement regarding a faulty example when the example is actually faultless.
These are fallacious refutations;
for by these the opponent's position is not truly refuted,
because that position is faultless.
Thus it is concluded.
Only the mere subject matter has been stated at the outset for the sake of establishing the general direction;
whatever reasoning or logic is involved here has been thoroughly examined elsewhere.
Thus ends the Nyāyapraveśaka-sūtra.
